subtitle: Red pork & hominy stew
verso: Corn that bursts into bloom: pozole for the fifteenth, its flavor fills the room!
story: Pozole goes back to pre-Hispanic Mexico, when cacahuazintle corn was cooked for ceremonies. In Jalisco it's red with guajillo and ancho, made with pork head or a mix of shoulder and bony cuts. It's what you make for September 15, Christmas Eve and New Year's. The broth should be brick red and thin, never a thick chili, and the garnish happens at the table.

ingredients.title: The meat
items: 2 lb pork neck bones or spine (espinazo)
2 pig's feet (manitas), split, optional but they give body
1 tbsp salt, plus more to taste

ingredients.title: The corn
items: 2 lb precooked cacahuazintle hominy (maíz pozolero, sold in bags at Mexican markets), rinsed, or 2 cans (29 oz each) hominy, drained and rinsed

ingredients.title: The chile
items: 1–2 chiles de árbol, optional, for heat
Pinch of cumin, only if your family uses it

ingredients.title: To serve
items: Finely shredded green cabbage, or lettuce as many tapatíos prefer

steps: Put the meats, onion and garlic in your biggest pot with the water. Bring to a boil and skim the gray foam for the first 15 minutes so the broth stays clean.

If using bagged hominy, add it now. Lower to a gentle simmer, partly covered, and cook 2 to 2½ hours, until the meat is very tender and the kernels have opened like flowers (revienta). Add the salt only once the corn has bloomed; salting early keeps it hard.
Meanwhile, stem and seed the chiles. Toast them on a hot comal 10–20 seconds per side, just until fragrant and pliable. Cover with hot water and soak 15 minutes.
Blend the chiles with the garlic, onion, oregano, cumin (if using) and [[1½ cups]] of the pork broth until completely smooth. Pour through a fine strainer, pressing with a spoon. Discard the skins.
Lift out the meat. Shred or cut it into bite-size pieces, pick the meat off the bones and feet, and return it to the pot. Discard bones, onion and garlic.
If using canned hominy, add it now. Stir in the strained chile and simmer 30 minutes. Season well with salt. It should be red and brothy, not thick.
Serve in deep bowls. Everyone garnishes their own: cabbage, radish, onion, oregano rubbed between the palms, chile piquín and a good squeeze of lime. Tostadas on the side.

pressureCooker.time: 45 min high pressure + 20 min natural release
steps: Toast, soak, blend and strain the chiles exactly as in the traditional method.
Put the meats, onion and garlic in the pot. Add bagged hominy now if using. Add water to the max-fill line (about 3½ quarts in an 8-qt pot; use about two-thirds of the meat in a 6-qt).
Seal and cook at high pressure 45 minutes (55 if using pig's feet). Let the pressure release naturally for 20 minutes, then vent.
Remove the meat, shred it, discard the bones and aromatics, and return the meat.
Switch to Sauté. Add the strained chile, canned hominy if using, and the salt (salt after the corn has bloomed). Simmer uncovered 20–30 minutes. Taste and serve.
pressureCooker.note: Plenty of grandmas already make pozole in a stovetop olla exprés. Count about 35 minutes from when the valve starts to rock.

tips: Strain the chile. The skins make the broth gritty and bitter.
Toast chiles until you smell them, only seconds. If they smoke, they'll taste bitter: throw them out and start over.
Pozole is better the next day. Chill it and lift off the fat if you like.
A weeknight version most families accept: bone-in chicken thighs instead of pork, about 1 hour on the stove.

variations.name: Pozole Verde
variations.subtitle: Green pozole with pumpkin seeds
variations.note: Thursdays in Guerrero are jueves pozolero. The green comes from pepitas, tomatillo and fresh herbs. The table gets chicharrón and avocado and, depending on the region, a raw egg cracked into the hot broth or sardines, with mezcal on the side.

items: Pork and hominy from the base recipe (or 1 whole chicken)
2 hoja santa leaves (or 1 tsp anise seed)
To serve: chicharrón, avocado, onion, oregano, lime, tostadas

steps: Cook the meat and hominy as in the base recipe, steps 1, 2 and 5 (add canned hominy now if using). Leave out the red chile.
Toast the pepitas in a dry pan, stirring, until they puff and pop but don't brown. Let cool.
Simmer the tomatillos and chiles in water 8 minutes, until olive green. Drain.
Blend the pepitas, tomatillos, chiles, onion, garlic, hoja santa, epazote, cilantro and romaine or radish leaves with [[2 cups]] broth until very smooth.
Heat the lard in a skillet and fry the green sauce 5 minutes, stirring.
Stir it into the pot and keep at a bare simmer 15 minutes. A hard boil makes the pepita sauce split.
Serve with the garnishes.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure times for the meat. Add the green sauce on Sauté-Low and don't let it boil.

variations.name: Pozole Blanco
variations.subtitle: White pozole
variations.note: The oldest style: pork, corn and salt in the broth, nothing else. All the chile is served on the side so each bowl is seasoned at the table.

items: Everything from the base recipe except the red chile
For the salsa: 10 chiles de árbol

steps: Cook the meat and hominy as in the base, steps 1, 2 and 5 (add canned hominy now if using). Skip the chile.
For the salsa, toast the chiles a few seconds, soak 10 minutes, blend with garlic, salt and water, and strain.
Serve the white broth with the salsa, onion, oregano, lime, cabbage and radish on the table.
variations.pressureNote: Same pressure times as the base recipe.
